Day 03 of 100 · AWS Networking Foundations

EC2

User-confirmed topic; original Day 3 artifact pending, although prior project conversation confirms EC2 + secure SSH focus.

The topic is now confirmed by the project owner, so the technical article is populated. The canonical ledger status is not promoted until the original published artifact is recovered.

EC2 introduced on-demand virtual servers and the practical connection between compute, images, instance types, storage, networking and secure remote administration.

Architecture / mental model

AMI + instance type + subnet + Security Group + storage + IAM role → EC2 instance → application / SSH administration

How it works

An EC2 instance is a virtual server. The AMI supplies the starting operating-system/software image, while the instance type defines the compute, memory and networking capacity available to the virtual machine.

Launching an instance is therefore a composition of choices rather than a single 'create server' button: Region and Availability Zone, subnet, IP addressing, Security Groups, storage, IAM role and key-based access all affect how the host behaves.

The Day 3 journey also focused on secure SSH access. Reachability requires the route and Security Group path to exist, but access should still be restricted to the intended administrative source instead of exposing SSH to the whole internet by default.

Hands-on reference

aws ec2 describe-instances --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,State.Name,InstanceType,PrivateIpAddress,PublicIpAddress]' --output table
ssh -i ~/.ssh/my-key.pem USER@PUBLIC_IP

Verification

Confirm instance state, subnet, Security Group and IP addressing in the API/console. Then connect using the intended SSH key from an allowed source and prove an unapproved source/path is not allowed.

Field note / gotcha

A running EC2 instance is not automatically reachable. Public IP assignment, subnet routing, Security Groups, NACLs and the guest firewall/service must all agree.

Security considerations

Restrict SSH, prefer Session Manager where appropriate, attach least-privilege instance roles rather than static credentials, patch the OS and protect IMDS access using current recommended settings.

What I learned

Compute is only one layer. A virtual server becomes useful when identity, network and operating-system controls line up around it.
